title: How SwiftUI works (declarative UI)
summary: In SwiftUI you describe what the screen should look like for the current state. When state changes, SwiftUI calls `body` again, compares the result with the old one and updates only what changed.
body: **In simple words:** In UIKit you give step-by-step orders: "create a label, set its text, when data changes update the text". That is **imperative**. In SwiftUI you say: "the screen is a label showing `name`". That is **declarative**. When `name` changes, SwiftUI updates the label for you.
**Formula to remember:** `UI = f(state)`. The `body` is that function.

**Views are cheap structs:** a SwiftUI `View` is not the actual pixels on screen; it is a lightweight description. SwiftUI creates them often and throws them away. The real, long-lived UI and your `@State` live in SwiftUI's internal storage.
**The update cycle:** state changes → SwiftUI marks views that depend on it as invalid → calls their `body` → diffs the new description with the old → applies minimal changes to the rendered UI.
**Modifiers** (`.padding()`, `.foregroundStyle()`) wrap a view in a new view. Order matters: `.padding().background(.red)` colours the padding too; `.background(.red).padding()` does not.
**Why it matters in interviews:** most SwiftUI questions (state, identity, performance) are really about this cycle: what triggers `body`, how often, and what SwiftUI thinks is "the same view".
keyPoints: Declarative: describe UI for a state; SwiftUI handles updates. `UI = f(state)`.
Views are value-type descriptions, recreated often; state lives in SwiftUI storage.
State change → body re-evaluated → diff → minimal UI update.
Modifier order matters because each modifier wraps the view.
Single source of truth: each piece of data has one owner; others read or bind to it.

mistakes: Doing work in `body` (network calls, sorting big arrays) - it can run many times.
Thinking a `View` struct is the on-screen object and storing references to it.
followups: **SwiftUI vs UIKit: when would you choose UIKit?** Very complex collection layouts, fine scroll control, advanced text editing, or when supporting very old iOS versions.
**Why is `body` called so often and is that bad?** It is cheap by design as long as `body` does no heavy work.
**What is `some View`?** An opaque return type: one concrete view type the compiler knows, hidden from you.
